gui.gonzotech.notes.title: Scholar's Notes
gui.gonzotech.notes.p1.title: Hello me
gui.gonzotech.notes.p1.body:
*"How do I put this... I — that is, you — am the old you. I wiped my, well, your memory. I don't plan on coming back: you're my living tombstone now. I hope you get a better life than I had... Good luck."*

Self — Gonzo:

Farewell, Gonzo...

To bring order to this mad world, the first thing I crafted was a chalkboard. It is My chief instrument of knowledge. Now I can see formulas before My eyes, balance equations, and make discoveries.

**By dragging blocks into an equation**, I immediately see the board's hints — it judges how precisely the elements are balanced.

If the balance accuracy **exceeds 90%**, it results in a full **Discovery**.

Here I can leave Myself notes and endlessly combine units, deriving new physical quantities. As I progress, the board will unlock harder problems and unknown constants.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p2.title: Observation
gui.gonzotech.notes.p2.body:
Watching the beasts, I noticed one strange thing: they often leave fruit in pits, grass or leaves and come back to it later.

Maybe something happens to the fruit in that time. I need to check.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p3.title: Fermentation
gui.gonzotech.notes.p4.title: Energy
gui.gonzotech.notes.p4.body:
Watching fire and water, I gradually arrived at one simple thought: in both cases energy can be obtained and transferred, if the process is organised properly.

To keep Myself from getting confused by the terms, I decided to call heat **GTH** (Gonzo Tech Heat), and pure energy — **GTU** (Gonzo Tech Units).

To begin with I need a stable source of GTH. So I assembled a firebox and tried to get heat out of ordinary burning. We shall see what can be done with it.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p5.title: Firebox and Boiler
gui.gonzotech.notes.p6.title: Stirling Generator
gui.gonzotech.notes.p6.body:
The firebox and the boiler work, but steam by itself is good for very little. I decided to try a Stirling engine.

The principle turned out to be fairly simple: a difference in temperature makes the pistons move, and that motion can already be used to obtain **GTU**.

The problem turned out to be elsewhere — the boiler constantly loses water. It has to be topped up by hand, and that gets tedious quite quickly.

So the next step is to return the water back into the system.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p7.title: Condensation
gui.gonzotech.notes.p7.body:
Gradually it became clear where the water goes. Steam leaves the system, cools down and no longer comes back on its own.

I assembled a condenser that cools the steam and returns the resulting water to the boiler. By rough estimates, every condenser gives 13% better water return efficiency in the cycle.

Now the water no longer has to be hauled by hand. There are still losses, but the system can already run almost without intervention.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p8.title: Closed Loop
gui.gonzotech.notes.p8.body:
Condensation noticeably reduced the losses, but did not solve the problem completely. Even in a closed system, water and energy are gradually consumed.

So I decided not to try to save every drop, but instead to spend part of the **GTU** on returning water.

For that I assembled an automatic first_pump. It draws water from an external source by itself and feeds it back into the system.

The result is a closed cycle. It needs a little energy to run, but no longer depends on a constant manual water supply.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p9.title: Electric Smelting
gui.gonzotech.notes.p9.body:
When there was enough energy, I wanted to use it not only for the operation of the system itself.

I assembled an energy first_accumulator and an electric furnace. The first_accumulator gradually discharges on its own, but I hope to fix that in the future. Compared to an ordinary furnace it runs cleaner and allows far more precise control of the heating…
gui.gonzotech.notes.p10.title: Logistics
gui.gonzotech.notes.p10.body:
When there were more machines, life without proper logistics became hard. To set up the network I made a wrench.

With it you can look at the contents of the connected pipes and change their mode. 
A normal **RMB** switches the flow direction: automatic mode, extraction or output. 
**Shift + RMB** is used to rotate the elements.

I divided the system itself into several types: wires for **GTU**, pipes for water and steam, and separate lines for **GTH**. To join several directions together I had to make distribution nodes.

All of it can be built fairly compactly, so the same network is easy to extend as new machines appear.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p11.title: Cobblestone Generator
gui.gonzotech.notes.p11.body:
I finally assembled a setup that produces cobblestone by itself and picks up some ores along the way.

At its core it is the same pairing of water and **GTU**, only the process is now fully automated.

It runs steadily enough, though stoppages do happen: lava crystallises into obsidian right inside the bucket, and the pickaxe hits hard inclusions and breaks. Apparently there are no ideal machines yet.

Even so, this is My first setup that can be left unattended for at least some time.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p12.title: Item Logistics
gui.gonzotech.notes.p12.body:
When there were more items in the system, a single resource network was no longer enough. I made separate item logistics with pipes, nodes and filters.

The filter lets through only what is set in it. For everything else I added a scavenger — it collects the excess items and sends them along a different route.

Now the loot can be split automatically right in the flow: what is needed goes to production, the rest — to processing or storage.

Nothing fundamentally complicated, but far less manual sorting.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p13.title: Item Logistics
gui.gonzotech.notes.p14.title: Universal Node
gui.gonzotech.notes.p14.body:
A separate node for each type of flow quickly began to take up too much space.

So I redesigned the scheme and assembled a universal node that can serve several kinds of flow at once.

The design came out noticeably more compact. Now all that is left is to properly solve the question of simultaneous load on several directions.

gui.gonzotech.notes.p15.title: Steam Turbine
gui.gonzotech.notes.p15.body:
The Stirling engine works, but the pistons have an obvious limitation: the motion comes out in fits and starts.

I decided to try a rotor design and aimed the steam straight at the blades. That is how the first version of the steam turbine came to be.

With several rotors it runs well, but you cannot keep adding rotors forever. At some point further expansion stops helping, and after that performance starts to drop.

So the size of the turbine has to be planned in advance, instead of just building it as large as possible…
gui.gonzotech.notes.p17.title: Machines and Redstone
gui.gonzotech.notes.p17.body:
I noticed the remarkable ability of redstone to read a machine's state through a comparator. Now the machine itself can report when it is full and when something in the system needs to change.

With that, one can automatically open gates, shut down individual machines, or keep accumulators from overflowing.

I am sure this remarkable red dust still holds many secrets...
gui.gonzotech.notes.p18.title: Ore Crusher
gui.gonzotech.notes.p18.body:
I wanted to get more useful material out of ore blocks than ordinary smelting gives, so I built a second_crusher.

It breaks the ore block and separates the metal from the additional materials. What is more, the result depends not only on the ore itself, but also on the rock it is found in.

That turned out to be a rather convenient way to obtain rare components alongside the main metal.

It seems that processing should account not only for the ore, but also for the place it was mined from.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p19.title: Grinder
gui.gonzotech.notes.p19.body:
A lot of metal dust is left over after processing. Throwing it away would be foolish, so I made a separate grinder for a similar process.

It crushes pure ingots into dust without impurities; this will be the basis for mixing…
gui.gonzotech.notes.p20.title: Simple Metallurgy
gui.gonzotech.notes.p20.body:
Steel turned out to be fairly easy to make from that very dust.

I mixed iron dust with coal and got steel dust. Then I assembled several more alloys the same way, simply changing the proportions of the starting materials.

That is how the first simple way to control a metal's properties through its composition appeared.

This is only the basic version. More complex alloys will need a separate process; some metals cannot simply be mixed in the right proportion and sent to a furnace…
gui.gonzotech.notes.p22.title: Press
gui.gonzotech.notes.p22.body:
I redesigned the Press so that the same body could perform several operations.

To do that I added two selector slots: one determines the shape, the second one presses.

The plate mold with a flat punch makes plates, the ingot mold can compress dust into an ingot, the core mold is needed for cores, and the wedge-shaped punch helps Me cut ingots into wires.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p23.title: Alloy Foundry
gui.gonzotech.notes.p23.body:
With alloys I wanted to go further. I began to look at metal not simply as a material, but as a set of separate properties.

Depending on the composition, strength, hardness, conductivity, heat resistance and other characteristics change.

For that I built the Alloy Foundry, which mixes several metals into one. The resulting properties depend on which components were used and in what amounts.

Even the colour comes from the composition, so the alloy itself already gives a rough idea of what it is made of.

Some combinations take enchantments poorly. Apparently, high inertness has a very practical downside...
gui.gonzotech.notes.p24.title: CF1UR Centrifuge
gui.gonzotech.notes.p24.body:
I built a second_centrifuge for a more detailed separation of ores.

Besides the main metal it extracts additional materials. That allows pulling far more useful components out of a single ore than ordinary processing does.

The process uses hot water, which can be obtained from steam, or — for emergencies — I provided electric water heating at the cost of **GTU**.

With caesium it is more complicated. Even the process of obtaining it remains dangerous, so that part of the production is best kept separate from the rest of the system.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p25.title: Second-Generation Machines
gui.gonzotech.notes.p25.body:
With the second generation of Machines I did not reinvent everything. The basic designs already work, so I simply boosted their throughput.

The new wires and pipes are made for larger flows, accumulators hold more energy, furnaces run faster, and item logistics handles bigger volumes.

It is the same technology, but now suitable for large production lines.

The next limitation is no longer an individual machine, but the organisation of the system itself.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p29.title: Advanced Steam Generator
gui.gonzotech.notes.p29.body:
I made the Advanced Steam Generator for situations where the ordinary steam setup is no longer enough.

It is based on several cores and heat exchangers. Thanks to them, more steam can be obtained from the same process, and the quality of the heat exchangers directly affects the result…
gui.gonzotech.notes.p30.title: The Heart of the Steam Generator
gui.gonzotech.notes.p30.body:
Precious blocks work excellently as heat exchangers; the sum of their heat resistance and conductivity directly affects the efficiency of the steam generator.

But here it is easy to overdo the design itself. If the heat exchangers are weak or there are too few of them, the setup starts consuming more resources than an ordinary cycle.

So this is not a universal replacement for the old system...
gui.gonzotech.notes.p31.title: Nuclear Firebox
gui.gonzotech.notes.p31.body:
After all the experiments with heat I finally assembled the nuclear firebox.

It allows obtaining a lot of **GTH** from a small amount of nuclear fuel. The more heat builds up inside, the more intense the operation becomes.

The main problem is overheating. At too high a temperature the risk to the surrounding blocks grows, and if nothing is done, the firebox itself starts to break down.

So the cooling system had to be designed together with the firebox from the start. To remove excess heat I made the tungsten absorber.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p32.title: Redstone and Lava
gui.gonzotech.notes.p32.body:
While experimenting with redstone I discovered another useful reaction.

If you direct a full bucket of lava onto a redstone block from a suitable side, both materials turn into **crimson obsidian**. The reaction does not happen from the top side.

Lava in a bucket behaves in a similar way when it touches water — the contents of the bucket turn into obsidian.

I do not yet know how widely this can be applied, but the reaction is worth keeping in mind.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p33.title: Tungsten, the Great Absorber
gui.gonzotech.notes.p33.body:
After the nuclear firebox tests I needed a separate heat storage. For that I converted the tungsten block into an absorber.

It connects to a heat pipe and takes excess **GTH** out of the system. Superdense ice can be placed next to it — it noticeably speeds up cooling.

The absorber itself has its limit too. When badly overheated it becomes dangerous for the surrounding area, so it should not be left unattended.

Right now this is the most convenient option for stabilising a nuclear system.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p34.title: Caesium, the Promise of an Explosion
gui.gonzotech.notes.p34.body:
Caesium turned out to be an extremely inconvenient material to work with.

I deliberately tested its interaction with water — the result was predictably bad. In water and when heated it explodes, and the dust left after processing behaves no better.

So a separate room for it had to be planned before production even started.

With caesium the main rule is simple: no accidental contact with water.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p35.title: The Fading of the Sun
gui.gonzotech.notes.p35.body:
The Sun stopped shining one day.

It did not happen like an ordinary sunset. The light simply disappeared and never came back. On Earth, on the Moon, on Mars — everywhere went dark.

I remember there were other people nearby, but I hardly remember their faces. We just looked up and tried to understand what was happening.

This entry is not about technology. I simply wanted to remember it.

And then I had to think about what to do next.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p36.title: The Fading of the Sun
gui.gonzotech.notes.p36.body:
After the crimson day I could not simply wait for the next one. It became clear: the Sun is not an eternal lamp but a resource, and it has a schedule.

I built a solar watch. It does not count time — it counts light: it shows the current day, how much is left until the next crimson day, and how well the panels are working right now.

Now, looking at the dial, I know whether I will finish My work before dark.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p37.title: Introduction to Deep Metallurgy
gui.gonzotech.notes.p37.body:
After the third discovery I began to understand metals far better, though before that I thought I had reached the limit of perfection. I can literally see how My ingot gained an exact numerical description: seven properties.

Strength — how much load the material withstands. More is better.

Brittleness — how easily it breaks. Here it is not «the more the better»: somewhere around 30 is a healthy margin, beyond that the material starts to crumble, but it mines faster and strikes sharper.

Inertness — resistance to rust, corrosion and dissolution.

Conductivity — how well the material carries electricity, or redstone signals.

Heat resistance — at what temperature it still holds its shape; above 75 the item no longer burns in fire and lava.

Ductility — how easily it can be pressed and bent, the counterpart of brittleness.

Weight — how heavy the same volume is. Heavy items also mine harder and hit harder, but the swing speed leaves much to be desired.

Separately — the mining level: the most I can dig through with it...
gui.gonzotech.notes.p38.title: Corten: Steel for Bad Weather
gui.gonzotech.notes.p38.body:
Ordinary iron does not last long outdoors — I needed an alloy that deals with rust on its own.

19 parts iron and 6 parts additives — 3 copper, 1 chromium, 2 nickel. 25 parts per smelt, 25 ingots.

Corten does not fight rust — it directs it. A dense layer of oxides grows on the surface, and the metal underneath is no longer eaten away. Hence the inertness of 86: rust reaches that layer and stops.

Strength 66, heat resistance 78, tier — iron. It sets no records, but rain and frost do not bother it.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p39.title: Stellite: The Strongest
gui.gonzotech.notes.p39.body:
I wanted to see how far strength could be pushed if expensive additives were no object.

6 parts cobalt, one each of chromium, tungsten, coal and neodymium — 12 parts, 11 ingots per smelt.

Strength 94 and heat resistance 96 — higher than anything I have created so far. Inertness 92. Tier — netherite and above.

It did not come cheap, but it is exactly what I wanted.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p40.title: Vitreloy: Metallic Glass
gui.gonzotech.notes.p40.body:
The idea was to make an alloy that solidifies faster than it can crystallise — then the structure stays glassy instead of lattice-like.

2 parts diamond, 2 ferromagnetic alloy, 3 zirconium and 2 nickel — 9 parts, 9 ingots per smelt.

It turned out surprisingly well: inertness 96 — it does not get higher, and conductivity 22 — nothing has lower. It bends poorly and hardly carries current, but heat resistance 89 with strength 92. Tier — diamond; this alloy will clearly become indispensable to Me for inert pipes carrying aggressive coolants.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p41.title: Semiconductor: The Basis of Electronics
gui.gonzotech.notes.p41.body:
Getting pure silicon for electronics is hard — almost all of it goes to waste, and only a grain remains.

One part neodymium, three parts pure silicon, two parts gold, one copper and three clay blocks, plus a radium nugget as a catalyst. And from that volume — only 4 ingots per smelt.

Its strength is so-so: 22, brittleness 66 — holding load is not for it. But conductivity 86, inertness 88, weight only 31: light and it does not rust. Heat, though, it does not like: heat resistance 55, and electronics and warmth are no friends at all.

Radium is the trace left after processing uranium and thorium ore, silicon — after diamond ore. Both via the second_centrifuge. Everything that «thinks» on contacts begins with this alloy...
tooltip.gonzotech.discovery_item: Use (RMB) to permanently unlock Tier %s recipes.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p26.title: Second-Level Logistics
gui.gonzotech.notes.p26.body:
The second generation of logistics had to be made first of all because of load.

I reinforced the wires and pipes, increased the throughput of the nodes and added the ability to properly split large flows between several directions.

The principle stayed the same, but now the network can be scaled without every expansion turning into another rework of the whole scheme.

For large setups this is already an almost mandatory upgrade.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p28.title: Item Logistics 2
gui.gonzotech.notes.p28.body:
With item logistics it turned out much the same.

First of all I gave the scavenger the ability to **delete** the items I no longer need. If you **power it with redstone**, it switches into **deletion** mode and burns everything the filter did not let through. I also increased the throughput of the pipes and nodes and kept the same filtering and sifting system, so that no new control logic had to be invented.

Old schemes are therefore easy to move over to the new version.

Now the extraction volume can be increased calmly, without constant manual sorting.
